note: Establish a blend-oriented baseline that captures most feed value with only six columns, then use stream compositions and costs to target improvements.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a six-column sequence making C4, C5, C6-paraffin and C6-naphthene blends plus C3s and heavier cuts; first assess splits, purity, and costs, then tune weak/costly columns and add high-value pure separations only if justified.
Step 1 baseline: root C4/C5; light train ethane/C3 then C3/C4; heavy train C5/C6, C6/C7, then paraffin/naphthene. Moderate stages/reflux and 10% pressure drops. Sell all leaves initially to expose composition and economics.

note: Sharpen the light-end and C5 splits so the C3, C4 and C5 blends can actually sell; heavy columns are unchanged for now.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a blend-first train (C3, C4, C5, C6 paraffin, C6 naphthene), then add valuable heavy pure products. Step 2: sharpen the C4/C5 root and C5/C6 split enough to make the three light blends sellable; then optimize heavy cuts and reduce costs.
Baseline at 3 reflux leaked ~30% C5 into the C4 cut and left C5 only 47% of BT, so no products sold. Root and B dominate separation quality. Increased root to 90/5, T to 60/5, TT to 50/4, B to 80/5. Kept heavy columns unchanged to isolate the effect and save solves.

note: Test stronger stripping at the C5/C6, C4/C5 and C3/C4 splits, plus ethane removal, to convert the four largest light streams into saleable blends.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a blend-first train (C3, C4, C5, C6 paraffin, C6 naphthene), then add valuable heavy pure products. Step 3: use higher boil-up to stop light-key leakage into bottoms, add an ethane-removal column for C3, and assess whether light blends and C6 paraffin become saleable.
Current 90/5/5 root and 60/5/5 T still leak large amounts of C5 into B and n-butane into TB. TT has 11% n-butane in its bottoms and TTT has 12% ethane. Reboil ratio should strengthen stripping: raise root/T/TT/B boil-ups. TTT 35/2/3 follows agent-7's successful C3 strategy. Heavy columns held fixed for diagnosis.

note: Abandon the costly light-end train and test a compact warm-end blend plant with C4/C5, C5/C6, and C6/C7 splits.
notebook:
PLAN: Rebuild around the valuable warm C5/C6 blends: discard C4- at the root, recover a C5 blend, then split C6 from C7+ and assess a paraffin/naphthene column. Step 1: establish clean C4/C5, C5/C6 and C6/C7 cuts with only three columns.
Agent-7's 60/5/2 root makes a good C4/C5 cut and costs $177M, versus my bloated $466M root. The light train is uneconomic. Their B at 55/3/3 puts too much C6 overhead, so use 60/4/2 for the C5/C6 split. BB at 55/3/2 should yield a C6-rich tops stream. Avoid pure close-boiling products unless blend economics fail.

note: Sharpen the C4/C5 and C5/C6 cuts and add a C3/C4 splitter so the three light blends can finally sell.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a saleable light-blend train first: sharp root C4/C5 cut, C3/C4 split, sharp C5/C6 cut, then C6/C7 cut. Step 2: achieve actual 95% blend specs and positive cash flow before adding a C6 paraffin/naphthene split.
Prior low-reflux cuts were far from spec. Agent-7 showed 80/6/3 lifts C5 blend to 82%; root butane leakage and DMB overhead remain. Use 80/8/3 root and 90/8/3 C5 column. A 50/4/2 C3/C4 splitter should monetize both light blends. C3+C4+C5 blend revenue is about $850M/yr, enough to support a disciplined four-column train. BB is diagnostic for the later C6 paraffin split.

note: All four target blends sit at 84–86%, so make a decisive separation upgrade at every cut; successful specs would unlock about $1.49B/yr of blend revenue.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a saleable light-blend train first: sharp root C4/C5 cut, C3/C4 split, sharp C5/C6 cut, then C6/C7 cut. Step 2: achieve actual 95% blend specs and positive cash flow before adding a C6 paraffin/naphthene split.
All four current target streams are 84-86% blend, so separation—not topology—is the blocker. Root leaks ~94 mol/s butane into BT; T leaks C3 into TB and butane into TT; BB leaks pentane overhead. Raise all four splits decisively (100/12/5 root and C5, 70/10/5 C3, 80/10/5 C6). Potential four-blend revenue ~$1.49B/yr versus ~$0.8-1.0B cost, so this should cross into profit if specs are met. Avoid the failed 100/5/5 root pattern by using high reflux.

note: Remove the worthless C3/C4 branch and strongly strip the C5 column: its only major contaminant is dimethylbutane, so this directly targets the missing C5-blend purity.
notebook:
PLAN: Prioritize the two highest-value blend products (C5 and C6 paraffin) with a compact three-column train; first make the C5/C6 split meet 95%, then reduce root/C6 costs. I am testing stronger stripping in B.
The current C5 overhead already recovers essentially all 695 mol/s C5, but contains about 100 mol/s 2,2-dimethylbutane: C5 purity is 87%, so only downward DMB leakage prevents a ~$597M/yr sale. Root butane leakage is not the current blocker. Raising B boil-up from 5 to 10 should drive DMB into BB while retaining C5 overhead. C6 paraffin already sells for $714.5M/yr. The entire T branch earns zero and costs $79.5M/yr, so remove it. Keep the proven root and BB settings for this isolation test; three-column revenue potential is ~$1.31B/yr against ~$0.95B/yr current cost.

note: Restore the best valid design; the stronger stripping test severely degraded both target blends.
notebook:
PLAN: Restore the best four-blend train, then make one controlled upgrade at a time and prune any branch whose revenue cannot cover its cost. Current step: recover the -0.719 design after the excessive B boil-up experiment failed.
The 100/12/10 B column was counterproductive: BT fell to only 58% C5 with heavy C6 leakage, so 10 is far beyond the useful stripping range. BBT also fell to 92% C6 paraffin. Current three-column costs ($1.08B/yr) are too high for zero revenue. Best prior design had all four blends around 84–86%, implying the limitation is cut sharpness rather than product value. Need avoid further simultaneous wholesale changes. Other visible plants are also unprofitable; high reflux/stages and cold light-end columns are expensive. C5 and C6 paraffin remain the highest-value compact targets.

note: Switch to a compact heavy-end plant: recover the octane/nonane cut, then split it into two high-purity products without any refrigerated light-end columns.
notebook:
PLAN: Abandon the expensive light-blend train and test the compact heavy-end business first: isolate octane+nonane, then split them into two premium pure products. If profitable, tune costs/purity and consider adding heptane recovery.
All prior C3–C6 blend attempts were unprofitable, with three-column costs around $1.08B/yr and products only 84–86% even after upgrades. Strong stripping (B=100/12/10) also caused severe C6 leakage. The heavy end needs only a sharp C7/C8 cut and an easy C8/C9 split, avoiding refrigerated light-end columns. Octane and nonane are worth $359M and $104M/yr at base purity, with 20% premiums at 99%. Start with moderate 45- and 40-stage columns to learn purity and cost.

note: The previous root column made a C5/C6 cut, not the intended C7/C8 cut. Strongly increase boil-up to drive heptane and everything lighter overhead, then split the small octane/nonane bottoms stream.
notebook:
PLAN: Abandon the expensive light-blend train and test the compact heavy-end business first: isolate octane+nonane, then split them into two premium pure products. If profitable, tune costs/purity and consider adding heptane recovery.
The prior root cut was far too light: its bottoms still held 2184 mol/s rather than the desired 295 mol/s of C8/C9. Move the cut decisively by raising root boil-up from 3.5 to 12 and stages to 70, while retaining enough reflux for a C7/C8 split. The easy octane/nonane splitter uses 45 stages and ratio 4. All earlier C3–C6 blend trains were unprofitable and missed purity. Octane/nonane base revenue is $463M/yr, potentially $556M at premium purity.

note: Make the C7/C8 split with high reflux and low boil-up, then separate the resulting octane/nonane bottoms into the two saleable products.
notebook:
PLAN: Build a compact heavy-end business: root removes C6 and lighter, B makes the C7/C8 cut, and BB separates octane from nonane. First obtain saleable purity, then reduce root cost and tune the split.
Root at 70/4/12 puts essentially all C7+ in B but costs $449M/yr and still admits C6. B at 45/4/4 made the wrong cut (C6 overhead, mixed C7/C8 bottoms). Use low boil-up and high reflux in B to reject heptane overhead while retaining octane/nonane below. Reduce root to 50 stages to cut capital. Add a moderate octane/nonane splitter. Potential C8+C9 base revenue is $463M/yr, $556M/yr premium. Earlier light-blend trains all missed 95% purity and lost money.

note: Use the team's cheapest promising C5-rich stream and add a dedicated C5/C6 finishing split; success would finally produce substantial blend revenue.
notebook:
PLAN: Switch to the most economic credible route: copy R484's low-cost C4/C5 root and C5/C6 pre-cut, then add one finishing column on BT to sell the C5 blend. If it meets 95%, reduce cost and polish; otherwise make one decisive purity correction.
R484 root 80/8/4.5/0.2 rejects C4 overhead and B 60/6/1 gives BT with 77% C5, 11% DMB, 8% 2MP. A third C5/C6 splitter should recover about $600M/yr of blend. R484 total cost is only $414M/yr, unlike my heavy train ($566M with no sales). Earlier attempts show excessive boil-up contaminates tops with C6; BT needs a controlled C5/C6 cut. Heavy-end trains have not produced purity and are abandoned.

note: Cut the root's capital and refrigeration burden while strengthening the C5 finishing split to recover some of the 111 mol/s N-pentane currently lost in BTB.
notebook:
PLAN: Keep the only route that has produced revenue—the C5 blend from BTT—but cut the dominant root cost and increase blend recovery. Step 1: reduce root stages/reflux and pressure, while adding separation to BT so more C5 can go overhead without C6 contamination. Step 2: use the remaining solves for the largest observed cost/purity bottleneck.
Current R484-derived plant sells 154 mol/s of 99% C5 blend for $136M but costs $445.5M. Root alone costs $332.6M; the 80/8 refrigerated column is not justified by this small product. BTB still contains 111 mol/s N-pentane, so a stronger 80/8/5 finishing column may recover substantially more blend. Earlier heavy-end routes made no sales and are abandoned.

note: Aggressively reduce the dominant root cost and downstream capital while retaining the two proven saleable blend cuts.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the only selling BTT C5 and BTB C6 products while aggressively cutting root and downstream costs. Step 1: test a much smaller, very-low-pressure root and smaller downstream columns. Step 2: if purity survives, trim further; otherwise spend the last solves restoring the best product split with lower cost.
Only this R484-derived route has revenue. Previous root cost $344M of $462M total, dwarfing $308M sales. Root dp=0.5 and 50/5 are therefore the main target. Lower pressure should reduce refrigeration and diameter-related cost; fewer stages cut capital. B and BT also need cheaper sizing. Heavy-end and light-blend routes repeatedly yielded no sales and are abandoned. Five solves remain, so prioritize one coherent low-cost test rather than another new topology.

note: Restore the only strong-revenue design and test a single dominant-cost lever: much lower root pressure, while retaining its proven separation settings.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the best proven two-product flowsheet and spend the final solves only on reducing its dominant root cost. Step 1: restore the best valid design and raise only the root pressure drop to 0.8, retaining its 50/5/4.5 separation settings. Step 2: if the products survive, finish; otherwise revert to the best valid design.
The best R484-derived plant had about $308M revenue and $462M cost, with the root responsible for roughly $344M. The latest aggressive 30-stage/3.5-reflux root destroyed the C5 sale, so separation settings must be retained. Higher pressure drop is the last targeted cost lever. Other routes repeatedly failed to sell anything and are abandoned.
